content.text: 100% is the wrong reliability target. Past a certain point users can't tell the difference, every extra nine costs more than the last, and a target with no room for failure leaves no room for change. Measure what users experience with an SLI, set an SLO a little below perfect, and treat the gap, the error budget, as something you spend on releases, with a policy for when it runs out.

A team's status page shows "Uptime: 100%" for the quarter, measured by a probe that loads the home page every minute. Leadership makes it the goal for next quarter. Every incident now triggers a release freeze, deploys move to Sunday nights, and a database upgrade waits for months. Meanwhile, support forwards complaints about failed payments that never show up on the uptime chart: the home page kept loading the whole time.
The common misconception
The belief: the reliability goal for any service should be 100% uptime. Anything lower is planning to fail, and a professional team doesn't plan to fail.

It's a reasonable instinct. Outages are painful, public and expensive, and the SRE book itself warns that "unreliable systems can quickly erode users' confidence." Contracts and status pages talk in nines, so more nines sounds like more quality. And nobody wants to stand in front of customers and say "we plan to fail".

The half-truth: reliability matters enormously, and you should know exactly how reliable you are. But 100% is neither reachable nor useful as a target, and chasing it costs you what users actually value.
What actually happens
Past a point, users can't see the extra nines

Google's SRE book puts it bluntly: "a user on a 99% reliable smartphone cannot tell the difference between 99.99% and 99.999% service reliability!" The user's network, device and everything in between fail more often than your extra nine would. Meanwhile the cost isn't linear: "an incremental improvement in reliability may cost 100x more than the previous increment." So the book treats an availability target "as both a minimum and a maximum": exceeding it by a lot wastes chances to ship features, pay down debt or cut costs.
100% leaves no room for change

The SRE workbook adds the other half: "The number one source of outages is change." New features, security patches, hardware and scaling all put a 100% target at risk, so "an SLO of 100% means you only have time to be reactive." A team that truly holds 100% can never update its service.
SLI, SLO and error budget
A
service level indicator

is "a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided." The workbook recommends writing it as a ratio: "the number of good events divided by the total number of events", such as successful HTTP requests over all requests. A
service level objective
is "a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI." For latency SLIs, the target is a
percentile
, for the reasons in our article on average latency.
The
error budget

follows directly: it's "100% minus the SLO." The workbook's example: with a 99.9% success SLO and 3 million requests in four weeks, the budget is 3,000 errors, and an outage that causes 1,500 of them "costs 50% of the error budget."
The budget is a decision tool

In the SRE book's practice, "as long as there is error budget remaining", new releases can be pushed. When it's spent, "releases are temporarily halted" while effort goes into reliability. The speed of spending matters too. Burn rate is "how fast, relative to the SLO, the service consumes the error budget": a burn rate of 1 leaves "exactly 0 budget at the end of the SLO's time window." That turns alerting from "any error" into "the budget will run out soon".

content.text: The SRE book's advice: "It's better to start with a loose target that you tighten than to choose an overly strict target that has to be relaxed when you discover it's unattainable." Base the first SLO on what you measure today, and consider a tighter internal SLO than the one you promise users, as a safety margin.

blocks.title: An SLO without a policy is just another chart

content.text: The workbook is explicit: without stakeholders committed to acting on the budget, "SLO compliance will simply be another KPI (key performance indicator) or reporting metric, rather than a decision-making tool." Write down what happens when the budget runs out, and get product, development and operations to sign it before you need it.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Pick one or two SLIs users would recognize

content.text: Start with the success ratio and the latency of your most important requests, measured where users meet the service, such as the load balancer, not by a probe on the home page.

items.title: Set the first SLO from your data

content.text: Look at the last four weeks; the workbook calls a four-week rolling window "a good general-purpose interval". Set the target near what you already achieve, so it describes reality before you try to change it.

State what changes when the budget is spent: for example, only fixes and reliability work ship until it recovers. The workbook suggests the approval itself is "a good test for whether the SLOs are fit for purpose".
The workbook recommends paging at 2% of the budget spent in one hour or 5% in six hours, and a ticket at 10% in three days. Single errors stop waking people up; fast budget loss still does.
Key takeaways

items.text: 100% is the wrong target: users can't see the extra nines, each one costs far more, and it forbids change.
An SLI is good events over valid events; an SLO is the target for it over a window, below 100%.
The error budget is 100% minus the SLO, times your traffic: the failure you can afford to spend.
Use the budget to decide: ship while it lasts, focus on reliability when it's gone, and alert on burn rate.
Without a written, agreed policy, an SLO is just another number on a dashboard.
